---
title: Secure links
description: Signed, expiring links that open one form in one environment.
---

A secure link is a compact signed token that opens one form. The admin creates it, a URL carries it,
and the portal redeems it once to start a session.

## The token

Two segments separated by a single dot: the payload, then the signature.

```
base64url( canonicalJson( claims ∪ { purpose } ) ) "." base64url( HMAC-SHA256 signature )
```

There is no header segment. The algorithm is fixed, so nothing is negotiable and there is no
algorithm-confusion attack surface.

A link token carries four claims.

| Claim       | Meaning                                                             |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `formId`    | the single form this link opens                                     |
| `linkId`    | the stored link row, so storage can revoke and enforce one-time use |
| `expiresAt` | hard expiry in ISO 8601 UTC; valid strictly before this instant     |
| `oneTime`   | optional single-use marker, carried for the verifier                |

The payload is encoded, not encrypted: anyone holding a link can decode and read its claims. That is
why no personal data ever goes in a token. Claims are opaque ids and an expiry.

## Creating a link

```sh
curl -sX POST "$API/admin/forms/frm_auto_quote/links" \
  -H "x-qcms-internal-token: $INT" -H "x-qcms-admin-session: $ADM" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"expiresAt":"2030-01-01T00:00:00.000Z","oneTime":false,"count":1,"environment":"prod"}'
```

The response carries one entry per created row: `linkId`, `environment`, `url` and `expiresAt`.

- `environment` is required and has no default. A script that omits the field and silently gets a
  production link is the failure that rule exists to prevent.
- `count` defaults to 1 and is capped at 100. A larger batch is rejected before any row is written.
- `expiresAt` must be a future instant.
- Every route is form-scoped and environment-scoped, so a cross-form or cross-environment id takes
  the same not-found answer as an unknown link.

`GET /admin/forms/:id/links` lists one environment's links with a derived state of `active`,
`consumed`, `expired` or `revoked`. `POST /admin/forms/:id/links/:linkId/revoke` revokes one.

## The URL

The link URL is `${QCMS_PORTAL_BASE_URL}/l/<token>` for production, and
`${QCMS_PORTAL_BASE_URL}/<env>/l/<token>` for every other environment. The portal's redemption entry
calls the API to start a session.

Redemption checks the prefix against the link's environment and refuses a token presented under the
wrong one. That is a not-found answer, raised before the link's own state is read and before
anything is spent, and it names no other environment.

The environment lives on the stored row and never in the token, so a leaked token discloses nothing
about where it leads.

## Verification

Checks run in a fixed order: malformed, then bad signature, then wrong purpose, then expired, then
wrong form.

A verified signature is never sufficient on its own. The API must also consult the stored link row
for revocation and for atomic one-time consumption. Verification uses WebCrypto and compares in
constant time.

Once a link is verified the API starts a session, and from then on the session token is the
credential.
A secure-link session expires with its link, never after it.

Secure links are the one deliberate case of a token appearing in a URL, mitigated by expiry plus
that server-side row.

## Rotating the signing key

`QCMS_LINK_KEYS` is a comma or whitespace separated list, each entry at least 32 bytes. The first
entry signs new links; every entry verifies. Generate one with `openssl rand -base64 32`.

1. Prepend the new key and redeploy.
2. Keep the old key listed until every link signed with it has passed its longest expiry.
3. Drop the old key.

For a compromise, skip the grace period: drop the compromised key immediately, accept that
outstanding links die, and create replacements.

:::caution[Keep link identity opaque]
Do not encode personal data in how you distribute links, such as a per-recipient link identity that
itself embeds a name or email. The link identifier survives erasure by design.
:::
